WITH film_actor_counts AS (
  SELECT f.film_id, COUNT(fa.actor_id) as actor_count
  FROM film f
  LEFT JOIN film_actor fa ON f.film_id = fa.film_id
  GROUP BY f.film_id
),
avg1 AS (
  SELECT AVG(actor_count) as value
  FROM film_actor_counts
),
above_avg1 AS (
  SELECT fac.film_id, fac.actor_count, a1.value as avg1_val
  FROM film_actor_counts fac
  JOIN avg1 a1 ON 1=1
  WHERE fac.actor_count > a1.value
),
avg2 AS (
  SELECT AVG(actor_count) as value
  FROM above_avg1
),
above_avg2 AS (
  SELECT f1.film_id, f1.actor_count, f1.avg1_val, a2.value as avg2_val
  FROM above_avg1 f1
  JOIN avg2 a2 ON 1=1
  WHERE f1.actor_count > a2.value
)
SELECT
  SUM(actor_count) as sum_actors,
  AVG(actor_count - avg1_val) as avg_excess_over_avg1,
  AVG(actor_count - avg2_val) as avg_excess_over_avg2
FROM above_avg2;

assumptions.assumption: When either average is NULL (e.g., if no films exceed the first average), the aggregates in the final SELECT will naturally return NULL, representing the 'keep no films' condition. This relies on SQL's aggregate behavior over empty sets.
'Ignoring missing values' means leveraging SQL's built-in AVG() semantics, which excludes NULLs. Since COUNT(fa.actor_id) never produces NULL, this is mainly precautionary.
